about.title: About Me
about.body: I am Vinicius, 19, living in Santa Cruz de la Sierra, Bolivia. I build backend and web logic end to end — HTTP contracts, business rules, authn/authz, data — and I also read systems at a low level and security. Three axes of the day: serious technology, offensive and defensive cybersecurity, and Jewish halakha as a practical standard. I am not a one-tool niche: I design the service, harden it, and understand how it breaks.

pillars.craftBody: I start from how a program holds state, talks on the network, and defends itself. In backend and web logic I design APIs, data models, sessions/JWT as contracts, jobs, and observability. In C++20 and RE I work memory, binaries, and overlays that must stay stable under load. On offense I map real failures on endpoints and surface; on defense I close the same path with controls, integrity, and telemetry. I also read markets and chain. Grey-hat here means studying offense to design defense — not publishing recipes.
pillars.craftRepel: I design the service. I test it. I close it.
pillars.faithBody: In Santa Cruz de la Sierra, learning and the practice of halakha are not a footer. They are the other standard of the same day. Halakha sets the rhythm; the craft is measured with the same seriousness. בעזרת השם, כל עכבה לטובה — every delay is for the good.

items.title: Backend and web logic
items.body: I design and ship backend: HTTP contracts, business rules, authentication and authorization, persistence, and clear layer boundaries. Web logic is not empty CRUD: it is the system that must be correct under load and under abuse.

items.title: API security
items.body: I review APIs and endpoints as attack and defense surface: authn/authz, poorly scoped objects, flow abuse, secrets, rate limits, and trust chains. I document the failure and the fix — not an exploitation playbook.

items.title: Offense and defense
items.body: Both sides of the same problem. Offense: surface, logic, and binaries to see where a system yields. Defense: controls, integrity, and telemetry so that path stops being usable. Blind defense does not work.

items.title: Fernet
items.body: Fernet is custom C++20 tooling on Windows clients: high-performance overlays, process-state readouts, and integrity under load. It is how I study where a client holds, where the surface yields, and how to close it — defense and reverse-engineering research, not an offensive catalog or abuse recipes.

security.title: Audit and incident response
security.lede: When an attack already happened — or when you need to show how entry would have worked — I reconstruct the path: vector, observed methods, endpoints touched, data at risk, and what to close. An actionable report, not an exploitation playbook.

phases.title: Containment and evidence
phases.body: Isolate the active surface, preserve logs, tokens, and artifacts without trampling the scene. Stop the bleeding first; explain second.

phases.title: Timeline and entry vector
phases.body: Order what happened and when: abused credential, stolen session, IDOR, poorly scoped flow. The “how they got in” has to be defensible.

phases.title: Surface: endpoints and auth
phases.body: Map authn/authz, poorly scoped objects, flow abuse, and trust chains. Which endpoint returned what, under which identity.

phases.title: Impact and risk range
phases.body: Classify exposed data (PII, tokens, records, secrets) and severity from low to critical, with a clear rationale for business and engineering.

phases.title: Close and report
phases.body: Revoke, rotate, patch controls, add alerts, and deliver a report that states what happened, what was or could be stolen, and what still needs hardening.

case.title: API with poorly scoped object access
case.summary: Reconstruction of a typical REST API incident: an actor abused a predictable identifier and an export endpoint with incomplete authz. Not a real client; this is the report format I deliver.
case.vector: Valid support-role session plus access to other tenants’ resources via IDOR on resource identifiers.
methods: Abuse of read and export endpoints
case.dataImpact: Account PII (name, email, attached documents), export metadata, and session tokens potentially reusable until rotation.
case.risk: High to critical — multi-tenant exposure of personal data and bulk extraction via export.
case.response: Mass revocation of sessions for the affected role, rotation of signing secrets, tenant-scoped authz hardening on all three endpoints, export rate limits, alerts on ID enumeration, and review of access logs in the incident window.

faq.metaDescription: Frequently asked questions about security audits, incident response, full-stack, frontend, and backend work.
faq.title: Frequently asked questions
faq.lede: Short answers for people evaluating an audit, post-incident response, or a build engagement. If something is missing, write.

items.a: It depends on scope. A security audit is not priced like a product build. Work can be billed hourly or as a fixed project once the scope is clear. Currency is US dollars (USD).
In USD. Hourly or fixed project, as agreed. Deposit and payment milestones are set when scope is locked; there is no public fixed rate without a brief.
It depends on complexity, the access you provide, and the kind of work (audit, incident response, or build). Small scopes close faster; larger ones ship in milestones.
We re-quote. Extra hours or a project addendum; scope creep is not absorbed silently. Better to say it early than stretch the same price.
A serious message with the problem, the stack, and the outcome you want. We agree scope, billing (hourly or project), and a work window. I reply after Shabbat.

items.q: When do you reply? What about Shabbat?
items.a: While observing Shabbat, the craft rests. Profiles can be read; mail is not opened until Motzaei Shabbat. After that, I reply in earnest.
Spanish and English. Based in Santa Cruz de la Sierra, Bolivia; when I give Shabbat or other cutoffs, I use Argentina time (as on the site note).

items.q: Is there confidentiality or an NDA?
items.a: Yes. Work is under agreement. Reports and findings go only to the authorized client. I do not publish real client cases or client data on the portfolio.
Yes. Based in Santa Cruz de la Sierra; the craft is remote unless the work requires presence.

items.q: How does this relate to Mercav.lat?
items.a: Mercav.lat is the role and the product. Audit, incident-response, or build engagements are agreed separately: they are not Mercav customer support or a marketplace help channel.
Delivery closes the agreed scope; it does not include open-ended support. Ongoing maintenance or iterations can be hired hourly or as a separate package.

items.q: Who is this for — and who is it not for?
items.a: For teams and products that want a service that closes cleanly, a serious audit, or post-incident response with an actionable report. Not for offensive catalogs, cheats, or “break X for me” without a defensive mandate and clear authorization.
Surface review (APIs, authn/authz, flows), findings prioritized by risk, and a remediation-oriented report. I document the failure and the fix — not an exploitation playbook.

items.q: What do you need from the client?
items.a: Agreed access (staging or scoped prod), a map of relevant endpoints or repos, and a technical contact. Without that, scope and timeline inflate.
I do not deliver offensive catalogs or recipes to break third-party systems. Grey-hat here means studying offense to design defense.

items.q: What do you deliver after an incident?
items.a: Timeline and entry vector, observed methods (patterns, not payloads), endpoints involved, data at risk, severity range, and a containment-and-close plan.
Containment and evidence first; reconstruction and report second. The window depends on severity and how much access the team gets.

items.q: Does it help if the attack already happened?
items.a: Yes. Post-incident work reconstructs what happened, what was exposed, and what to harden so the same path stops being usable.

items.q: What does a full-stack engagement cover?
items.a: Backend and web logic (HTTP contracts, domain, auth, data) plus the UI needed for the product to close. One profile that designs the service and understands how it breaks.
Fixed project when scope is closed, or hourly when scope is evolving. Timeline follows complexity and client dependencies. Currency is USD.
Yes, when the scope is UI, accessibility, and consuming defined APIs. If the backend is weak, I say so early: UI does not hide broken authz.
TypeScript and React / Next when it fits. I adapt to the product stack when API contracts are clear.
Yes: APIs, authn/authz, domain, persistence, jobs, and clear layer boundaries. Also low-level C++20 when the problem calls for it.
Code and contracts that hold under load and abuse, with explicit auth and data limits. Endpoint and design notes when the project needs them.
